q: What is the pathology of achalasia?
o: Failure of LOS relaxation and loss of peristalsis from degeneration of the myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus
why: Progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation and nocturnal cough.

q: What is the gold standard investigation for achalasia?
why: Barium shows a bird’s beak; endoscopy excludes pseudoachalasia from malignancy.

q: What is the main anaesthetic concern in achalasia?
o: Aspiration from a dilated oesophagus full of food and secretions
why: Consider clear fluids for days pre-op, emptying the oesophagus, head-up RSI or awake fibreoptic intubation.

q: What sign is classically seen on barium swallow in achalasia?
why: A dilated oesophagus tapering to a narrow LOS.

q: Which treatment is used temporarily in high-risk patients with achalasia?

q: Why is TPN usually given via a central line?
o: Its high osmolarity causes peripheral thrombophlebitis

q: What is the key electrolyte abnormality in refeeding syndrome?
why: Can cause arrhythmia, cardiac failure and death.

q: Systemic sclerosis is relevant to food bolus because of:
